title: Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
shortTitle: Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
summary: Reflection amplification is denial of service in which the adversary never sends the bulk of the traffic; innocent third party servers do. The attacker sends a request to a reflector service with the victim's address forged as the source, so the reflector's reply is delivered to the victim. When the response is much larger than the request, the technique amplifies the attacker's bandwidth by orders of magnitude, and well known amplification vectors have historically included domain name system, network time protocol, and memcached services, the last famous for extreme response to request ratios. Attackers scan for reachable reflectors, which means defender visibility may exist on both sides: the victim sees a surge arriving from many unconnected third parties, and the reflector operator sees huge numbers of short spoofed requests leaving. Signals that separate this from legitimate service use include inbound traffic from well known public services the organisation never queries, source ports indicating the response to a request nobody in the network made, responses with no matching outbound request in flow logs, and a very high ratio of bytes to packets. Because the apparent source is a legitimate server, blocking by source address is counterproductive and can break real dependencies. The durable fixes are network hygiene: preventing your own systems from being usable as reflectors and deploying source address validation at the edge.

beginner.definition: Reflection amplification is a denial of service attack that uses other servers to send the traffic. The attacker sends small requests that pretend to come from the victim. The replies, which are much bigger, all arrive at the victim instead.
beginner.whyItMatters: The victim receives far more traffic than the attacker could send alone. The servers sending the traffic are ordinary and innocent, so blocking them is difficult. Anyone running an open service on the internet may be used as a helper without knowing it. This makes the attack both powerful and hard to trace back.
howItWorks: The attacker finds many internet servers that answer small requests with larger replies.
They send a request to each server but write the victim's address as the sender.
The servers send their replies to the victim, believing the request was genuine.
Because replies are much bigger than requests, the total traffic is multiplied.
The flood arrives from many ordinary servers that the victim never contacted.
The attacker only needs a small amount of bandwidth to start the whole flow.
beginner.example: Imagine writing postcards to hundreds of shops, signing each one with a neighbour's address. Every shop answers with a large parcel delivered to that neighbour. The neighbour's hallway fills with parcels they never asked for, while you only paid for postcards. That is reflection amplification, and the shops did nothing wrong.
takeaways: The attacker sends little; innocent servers send the flood to the victim.
Blocking the apparent sources breaks real services and does not help.
Responses with no matching request are the clearest detection clue.

objectives: Explain the roles of the attacker, the reflector, and the victim.
Describe why some protocols produce a large amplification factor.
Explain how spoofed source addresses enable reflection at scale.
Identify flow evidence such as unsolicited responses to spot an attack.
Explain why blocking apparent sources is the wrong response.
Describe network hygiene steps that make your systems poor reflectors.
